title: Verifier‑Grounded Generate–Verify–Repair for Intent→Configuration NetOps Tasks: a Paired Mininet Emulation Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study that measured whether a verifier‑grounded generate–verify–repair (GVR) loop reduces operationally detectable policy‑violation errors when a hosted LLM generates network configuration sequences from operator intent in a Mininet emulation. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics (the same sampled initial candidate was reused for baseline and guarded pairs), N=200 paired intents were executed across three vendor‑template families and four topology patterns. The guarded pipeline permitted deterministic validation and a single verifier‑triggered repair. Baseline success (no policy violation detected) was 196/200 (98%); guarded success was 200/200 (100%). The paired risk difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.02 (95% bootstrap percentile CI 0.005–0.04); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.125. Four validator‑triggered repairs were invoked (4 additional model calls total), giving mean extra model calls per intent = 0.02 and per avoided violation = 1.0. Because the preregistered primary inferential test was McNemar’s paired test, we present that as the primary confirmatory inference (p=0.125) and report the archived paired bootstrap CI as an auxiliary estimate while explicitly noting and explaining the apparent inconsistency between the two methods in small‑discordant‑count settings. All analyses, deterministic verifier traces, raw model outputs, and execution manifests are archived with the evidence bundle; key accounting values referenced in text are drawn from those artifacts.

sections.introduction: Large language models (LLMs) can assist intent→configuration translation in network operations (NetOps) but may produce syntax, topology, or policy violations with operational consequences. Prior prototype and cross‑domain work demonstrate that pairing generation with deterministic verifiers and limited repair loops (generate–verify–repair, GVR) reduces mechanically checkable errors when an appropriate oracle exists [1], [2], [3]. However, questions remain about scaling verifier‑grounded workflows across heterogeneous vendor templates and realistic topology patterns [4], [5]. We preregistered and ran a confirmatory paired experiment to estimate whether a verifier‑grounded GVR loop reduces operationally detectable policy violations relative to single‑shot LLM generation in a controlled Mininet emulation. Contributions: (1) a preregistered paired design under shared_initial_candidate semantics; (2) a provenance‑traced Mininet‑style emulation with 200 paired intents across vendor/template strata; (3) artifact‑grounded primary inference (exact McNemar) and paired bootstrap effect estimation; (4) deterministic validator traces and a concise explanation reconciling the primary test and the archived bootstrap CI.
sections.related_work: Surveys of LLM‑for‑NetOps and AIOps document rapid growth and recurring evaluation gaps (benchmark provenance, verifier integration) [4], [5]. Prototype studies show LLMs can produce draft configurations but often introduce syntax, topology, or semantic errors; verifier‑grounded repair and GVR architectures have been proposed and demonstrated in domain prototypes (code, domain programs, limited NetOps examples) [1], [2], [3]. Our study builds a preregistered, paired, provenance‑traced instantiation of the GVR pattern in a Mininet emulation to quantify mechanically detectable policy‑violation corrections and the model‑call cost of repairs in a stratified multi‑template setting.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and estimand: The study was preregistered as C1‑GVR‑multivendor‑2026‑v1 prior to any model calls. Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (probability that an intent yields zero operationally detectable policy violations under guarded minus baseline). Design and sampling: paired binary outcomes on N=200 unique intents (baseline and guarded per intent), stratified across 3 vendor‑template families and 4 topology patterns (12 strata). Sampling, exclusion, and analysis rules were fixed in the preregistration and archived. Model and generation semantics: all generations used the declared model identifier gpt‑5‑mini (execution manifest: model_configuration.json). The archived model configuration records temperature = null/unset; null/unset is not evidence of deterministic hosted‑model sampling and does not imply temperature=0. Generation semantics were shared_initial_candidate: exactly one sampled initial generation per pair was produced and reused by baseline and guarded. By design, any paired outcome difference can only arise from deterministic validation and the permitted single repair call in the guarded pipeline; the guarded condition does not replace or produce an independent first‑pass generation. Validator and repair: a deterministic netops validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) checked syntax, reachability/topology constraints, and encoded policy/ACL constraints; the guarded pipeline permitted up to one verifier‑triggered repair call when the validator produced a failing/ambiguous outcome. Execution budget and accounting: task_count=200, planned_episode_count=400 (baseline+guarded), maximum_model_calls=400, initial_generation_calls_per_task=1, maximum_repair_calls_per_task=1. The execution manifest and deterministic reconciliation (archived) record all provider call accounting and verifier traces (see execution_manifest and deterministic_reconciliation artifacts). Analysis plan: the preregistered primary test is McNemar’s paired (exact) test for the binary per‑intent success indicator; effect size reported as paired risk difference with paired bootstrap percentile CI (archive contains bootstrap_seed=1729 and 10,000 resamples). Primary inference follows the preregistration (McNemar); bootstrap CI is presented as an auxiliary estimator but interpreted cautiously given small discordant counts (see Results).
sections.results: Execution and provider accounting: execution completed as preregistered (completed_episode_count=400; complete_pair_count=200). Provider audit and deterministic reconciliation record hosted_model_call_event_count = 204. The model call accounting arises as: 200 shared initial generation calls (one per paired intent) + 4 repair calls = 204 total hosted calls (stage_counts from reconciliation: shared_initial_generation=200, repair=4). The reconciliation 'condition_counts' fields in the archived audit refer to staged provider events (shared vs repair) rather than episode counts; the episode accounting remains 400 completed episodes (200 baseline + 200 guarded) because under shared_initial_candidate semantics both episodes in a pair reference the same initial generation event. Primary outcomes: contingency from archived paired_contingency_table.csv: n11=196 (both succeed), n10=4 (guarded success, baseline fail), n01=0 (guarded fail, baseline success), n00=0 (both fail). Baseline success rate = 196/200 = 0.98; guarded success rate = 200/200 = 1.0; paired risk difference = 0.02. The preregistered primary confirmatory test (exact McNemar two‑sided) yields p = 0.125. Bootstrap effect estimation: the archived paired bootstrap (seed=1729, 10,000 resamples) produced a percentile 95% CI for the paired risk difference = [0.005, 0.04]; that CI is included in archived analysis artifacts. Reconciliation of inferential statements: because the preregistered primary inferential method is McNemar’s exact paired test, we report p=0.125 as the primary confirmatory result (no rejection at α=0.05). The archived bootstrap CI is an auxiliary estimate of effect magnitude; with sparse discordant counts (here 4 discordant pairs and zero discordant in the opposite direction) some resampling estimators can produce percentile intervals that exclude zero while an exact conditional test remains non‑significant. This methodological difference can produce the apparent contradiction observed here; analysts should prefer the preregistered exact test for hypothesis testing while treating the bootstrap CI as a descriptive bound that may be optimistic in very small‑discordant settings. Repairs and cost: four verifier‑triggered repairs were invoked (repair stage count = 4). Total model calls = 204 → mean model calls per intent = 1.02; mean extra calls per intent due to guarded repairs = 0.02. In this run, each avoided policy violation corresponded to one repair call (mean extra calls per avoided violation = 1.0). Missingness and deviations: no pairs were excluded; missingness summary and deterministic reconciliation report zero failed episodes and zero exclusions. All counts and seeds referenced above are present in archived artifacts (analysis/*.csv, execution/*.jsonl).
sections.discussion: Within the constrained Mininet emulation and under shared_initial_candidate semantics, a deterministic validator plus a single permitted repair corrected all observed mechanically detectable baseline policy violations at marginal model‑call cost (4 repairs across 200 intents). The preregistered primary hypothesis test did not reject (exact McNemar p=0.125). The paired bootstrap CI from archived analysis suggests a small positive effect but may be optimistic in sparse discordant settings; this inconsistency is methodological rather than arithmetic and is resolved by reporting the preregistered exact test as primary while preserving the bootstrap interval as an auxiliary descriptive estimate. Operational implication (bounded): when a reliable deterministic validator that provides localized, actionable feedback exists, modest verifier‑triggered repair budgets can address classes of mechanically checkable errors (syntax, reachability, ACL/policy encodings) with low call overhead; however, the magnitude and operational utility depend strongly on baseline failure prevalence and validator coverage. Limitations that impact generality are discussed below.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired experiment comparing single‑shot LLM generation to a verifier‑grounded GVR pipeline for intent→configuration tasks in a provenance‑traced Mininet emulation. Guarded GVR corrected all four observed baseline policy violations at the cost of four repair calls (mean extra calls per intent = 0.02), yielding a paired improvement of 2 percentage points (paired risk difference = 0.02). The preregistered primary inferential test (exact McNemar) produced p = 0.125 (non‑significant at α=0.05); the archived paired bootstrap percentile CI [0.005, 0.04] is reported as an auxiliary effect estimate but interpreted cautiously due to small discordant counts. These artifact‑grounded results show that deterministic verifier‑guided repair can correct mechanically verifiable faults in this emulation at low model‑call cost, but they do not establish production readiness or coverage of high‑level semantic misinterpretations. Future work should increase verifier coverage, evaluate multiple models and real vendor hardware, and scale sample sizes to better power small absolute improvements. References follow the manuscript body in conventional form below.

limitations: Scope limited to Mininet‑style emulation with synthetic, provenance‑traced intent→configuration tasks; results do not directly generalize to production hardware or live operational environments.
Single declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) was evaluated; multi‑model generality is not established.

Deterministic validator coverage was limited to mechanically checkable errors (syntax, reachability, ACL/policy encodings); high‑level semantic or specification misinterpretations outside the validator’s oracle may remain undetected.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics mean observed paired differences could only arise from validator‑triggered repair; this design does not measure effects of alternative generation prompting strategies or multi‑sample candidate selection.

The confirmatory effect size (2 percentage points) did not reach statistical significance at α=0.05 for N=200; larger samples or higher baseline failure prevalence would be needed to demonstrate small absolute improvements with high confidence.
